title: How Teachers Mess Up The Amazing Benefits Of Routines
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Drawing on an observation of a second-grade teacher hovering over her class during a slow, five-minute walk to lunch, Linsin argues that teachers who talk, direct, and fuss over every step of a routine are inadvertently training students into learned helplessness rather than the maturity routines are supposed to build. His central claim is that well-taught, independently-executed routines are one of the best available tools for developing purpose, focus, and responsibility in students — but only if the teacher steps back and lets students actually run them. He notes that even a teacher who is well-liked, hardworking, and proud of her reputation can still be undermining her students simply by doing too much for them. The concrete argument is that the destination of a routine (the lunchroom, the desks after a transition) is beside the point; the real value lies in the maturity and independence the routine is meant to cultivate along the way. He frames over-management of routines as a widespread, easy-to-miss habit that quietly saps students of the growth those same routines were designed to produce.
points: A teacher who talks, directs, and hovers throughout a routine is training students into learned helplessness rather than competence.
Well-run, independently-executed routines are framed as building maturity, focus, and habits that transfer directly to academic performance.
Even a well-liked, hardworking, reputationally excellent teacher can be undermining students simply by doing too much for them.
The point of a routine isn't the destination — it's the character lessons the routine is supposed to build along the way.
quotes: The students were relatively well behaved but distracted—staring off into the distance, bumping into each other, lost in thought.
Yet, spend a couple of hours on any school campus and most routines look just like this, even with much older students.
Which is a bright red flashing sign that the students are very effectively learning how to be helpless and dependent on others, even for the simplest things like walking to lunch or opening a laptop.
The truth is that routines are one of the best opportunities teachers have to impact students and change them for the better.
But her approach, her aggressively doing and doing for her students, was hurting them. It was holding them back.
Routines are a means to an end. But the end isn’t the lunchroom or their seats after a transition. It’s the lessons they offer, which when allowed and nourished by the teacher, can be profound.
